video_title: The AI Crash Is Over. Here's What Comes Next
gist: Jordi Visser calls the AI factor 'speed crash' over and the bottom in, citing a ~10% four-day Nasdaq rally, collapsing factor volatility, new all-time highs in IWM, the NYSE Composite and the equal-weight S&P, and ~50% earnings growth with no credit or index-vol contagion. He argues index puts no longer hedge an AI book because factor vol has structurally decoupled from index vol, calls peak gross leverage, and pairs that with a debasement thesis built on the first coordinated US-Japan yen intervention since 1998, a collapsing Truflation reading, and the weakest six-month aggregate payrolls since 2012 ex-COVID.

insights.claim: Jordi Visser declares the AI-factor 'speed crash' finished and the bottom in on a probability basis, saying he would be surprised if the lows are taken out because investors are far too bearish relative to the earnings growth that is coming.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames the AI-factor washout as a buyable cleansing event rather than the start of a bear market, with the prior lows as the risk-management line.
insights.quote: The speed crash has occurred, it's over. The bottom is in as far as I'm concerned on a probability basis. If we take out the lows, I'd be surprised, uh mainly because I continue to believe people are way too bearish relative to the reality

insights.claim: The four-day rally in the Nasdaq reached close to 10%, clustering with famous bottoms like Liberation Day, COVID and 2022, and the S&P's breakout from a three-month May-to-July pennant was 6% bigger than the entire prior range - a move Visser says is not something to fade, distinguished from the 2022 bear-market rally by price sitting above an upward-sloping 200-day moving average in 80%-plus of AI thematic names.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Thrusts above an upward-sloping 200-day historically mark durable bottoms; a breakout larger than the consolidation it came from favors continuation over reversal.
insights.quote: And guess what? The rally we had was 6% bigger than the entire range that we saw for that time period. That is not something to fade.

insights.claim: Breadth confirms a bull market rather than a narrow AI melt-up: every S&P sector is up on the year with the index +13%, IWM, the NYSE Composite and the equal-weight S&P all made new all-time highs in the same week, the DAX and FTSE broke out to all-time highs, and the KOSPI 200 is up 61% year-to-date with its technology sector up 116% after the collapse.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Global, broad-based new highs undercut the contagion case and support staying long beyond mega-cap US tech.

insights.claim: Despite factor volatility hitting 45-year highs on some measures, no contagion reached index or credit markets - the VIX is at its lowest since January, single-name vol has mean-reverted to pre-episode levels and the CDX index behaved just like the VIX - so investors who bought S&P puts lost on both direction and volatility, while the six-day collapse in tech-momentum realized vol shows funds are now hedged or de-grossed and vol-targeted funds and burned pods cannot re-lever into a low-volume summer rally.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Confirms a leverage/factor event rather than a solvency event, and sets up chase risk as underexposed managers face seasonality fears with no ability to re-lever.

themes.theme: Hedging AI With Factor Vol, Rate-of-Change and Breadth

insights.claim: Visser argues factor volatility has structurally decoupled from S&P index volatility because it embeds long-short gross leverage, so index puts no longer hedge an AI thematic book the way they used to.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reprices the hedging stack toward single-name, factor and dispersion hedges instead of cheap-looking index puts for AI-heavy portfolios.
insights.quote: using index puts is not going to work the way that it used to

insights.claim: Visser explicitly calls peak gross leverage - predicting long-short gross comes down over the next few years as AI compresses time, increases crowding and lowers factor Sharpe ratios - and expects factor vol, measured as an equal weight of momentum, value, quality and beta, to stay structurally elevated in a 25-30 range rather than returning to prior lows.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A multi-year de-grossing regime means more frequent violent factor unwinds, higher hedging costs and structurally lower returns for crowded quant and pod strategies.
insights.quote: I'm making the call that we are at peak gross leverage and that we will see leverage come down over the course of the next few years

insights.claim: Visser's replacement risk model combines a 50-day rate of change on his 100-name global AI thematic index with internal breadth: a roughly 50% move over 50 trading days guarantees a fall, risk starts growing above 20%, and the warning fires only when elevated rate of change coincides with breadth breaking down inside the 100 names - a system he built because the 252-day S&P rate-of-change recession model that flagged September 2007 is too slow in an exponential-innovation cycle.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable de-risking trigger for AI exposure that fired ahead of the July momentum break, when traditional macro lead indicators would have signaled too late.

insights.claim: Universal AI access to backtesting and portfolio optimization increases crowding and produces more bubbles, parabolas and speed crashes, compressing market time as well as economic time - Visser notes July was the worst month for momentum in his entire dataset - which makes terminal values harder to estimate and lets a company re-rate from a 30 PE to a 20 PE very quickly, as he says is happening to Google now.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Multiple compression is now a fast discrete event rather than a slow grind, so hedging cadence and rebalancing frequency must rise permanently.
insights.quote: AI compresses economic time, but it it may also compress market time. The month of July for momentum was worse than any year over the data that I have.

themes.theme: AI Demand Data, Compute Shortage and the Memory Bottleneck

insights.claim: Per Gavin Baker, the AI sell-off is disconnected from the quantitative data: he has found no real negative demand metric and not a single instance of deceleration, with GPU availability, GPU rental pricing and the spot price of DRAM all accelerating.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Gavin Baker
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable monitoring checklist - GPU rental prices, availability, DRAM spot - that must roll over before turning bearish on AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: Um not a single instance of deceleration, nothing. In fact, every metric rate is accelerating.

insights.claim: GPU rental economics are inflating rather than deflating: a B200 cluster that rented around mid-$2 per hour seven months ago is now expected to rent for just under $4 per GPU hour, undercutting the thesis that AI chips have short useful lives and will not survive their depreciation schedules.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Gavin Baker
insights.so_what: Rising rental rates validate hyperscaler depreciation assumptions and AI-infrastructure asset values, directly rebutting the obsolescence short case.
insights.quote: The same type of B200 cluster that rented around mid $2 per hour 7 months ago is now expected to rent for just under $4 per GPU hour.

insights.claim: Visser has bought a decent amount of Nvidia over the last three weeks, arguing it trades at the lowest forward PE of the past 10 years, has already taken its multiple compression, and benefits from Vera Rubin and token-per-watt requirements - a safer AI holding that will not double quickly but is among the best risk-adjusted ways to stay exposed.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit long with a valuation anchor: de-rated mega-cap AI hardware as the lower-beta expression of accelerating compute demand.
insights.quote: Nvidia actually, as we record this, is at the lowest forward PE of the last 10 years. I've bought a decent amount of Nvidia over the course of the last 3 weeks.

insights.claim: Visser argues compute will never be sufficient because adoption is still tiny - only a few hundred thousand of 8 billion people are running generative AI agents - so demand is exponential against a physical supply that scales linearly, and falling prices on older GPUs merely mean newer supply is briefly saturating demand ahead of adoption.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, building on Gavin Baker
insights.so_what: Frames compute as a structurally short commodity: own the physical build-out rather than betting on a capex air pocket.
insights.quote: Guys, I say it all the time. There will never be enough compute, ever. We will continually be building compute.

insights.claim: Elon Musk said on the SpaceX earnings call that the current limiting factor is memory, with memory output rising around 20% a year against demand rising 200% a year or higher - confirming Visser's June 'AI equals memory' paper that more compute cannot solve the bottleneck without more memory, especially once consumer AI agents scale.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, quoting Elon Musk
insights.so_what: A 10x supply-demand gap is the cleanest pricing-power setup in the AI supply chain; memory supply catching compute is the exit trigger to watch.
insights.quote: The limiting factor currently is memory. The memory output is increasing by around 20% a year. So, supply is increasing by about 20% a year. The demand is increasing by 200% a year, maybe higher.

insights.claim: The AI capex cycle is showing up in hard macro and corporate data: earnings growth near 50% with revenue growth at 15% across sectors since Q1 2025, margins up from 13% to 17% year-over-year, the PMI soaring from below 50 a year ago to almost 60, and Palantir commercial revenue accelerating from 54% to 64% to 149% year-over-year, taking Q2 revenue from $306 million to $764 million with 220 deals of at least $1 million and 78 of at least $10 million.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Revenue and margin acceleration rather than multiple expansion underwrites the rally, and Palantir's commercial prints are the best public proxy for enterprise AI adoption since Anthropic and OpenAI do not report.

themes.theme: Hyperscaler Capex Math and the Decay of Public Companies

insights.claim: Visser is not bullish on hyperscalers relative to the infrastructure trade because Goldman Sachs projections put group quarterly free cash flow turning positive far into the future, meaning Microsoft, Meta and Amazon keep spending in the hope revenue arrives while facing heavy competition, and cloud revenue alone will not be enough.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Favors picks-and-shovels AI infrastructure over hyperscaler equity, since the capex burn is a multi-year free-cash-flow drag.

insights.claim: Visser argues hyperscaler multiples deserve compression and their CDS deserve to be wider for justified reasons - they keep leveraging up and without new products get priced like a utility or real estate company - making CDS rather than equity puts the right instrument for anyone shorting the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific short expression, and a warning for credit buyers that the spread widening is fundamentally warranted rather than a mispricing to fade.
insights.quote: whether their businesses will be there is a question, and that's why their multiples should be compressed, and their CDS should be wider

insights.claim: Visser reads Jeff Dean's departure and Demis Hassabis moving to another area as evidence that top AI talent is getting frustrated by bureaucracy at big companies like Google, which released AlphaFold for free while spending heavily and taking on debt - leading him to be negative on all public companies by 2030 while AI-native new business formations go parabolic, an inflection he dates to the release of Opus 4.5.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A structural short on incumbent public-equity profit pools and an argument for private exposure to one-person AI-native companies, with talent exodus as the early warning on monetization gaps.
insights.quote: It's reason why I'm negative on all public companies by the time we get to 2030, the bureaucracy is going to be a killer.

insights.claim: Visser's 'two printing presses' framework holds that government money printing debases the unit you measure wealth in while the AI printing press dilutes the durability of the corporate claims you bought to protect that wealth - the joint case for abundant intelligence and scarce Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Justifies owning scarce assets over both cash and long-duration equity claims; the core logic linking his AI and crypto books.
insights.quote: Two printing presses running at once. One dilutes the unit you measure wealth in. That is the debasement of your money. The other dilutes the durability of the corporate claims you bought into to protect that wealth.

themes.theme: Yen Intervention, Warsh and the Fiscal Train

insights.claim: Visser reads the first coordinated US-Japan currency intervention since 1998 as a Treasury-market defense: Scott Bessent is helping the BOJ so Japan does not have to sell its large Treasury holdings to buy yen, and is leaning on the Fed to help defend the yen and expand facility capacity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If the US is defending the yen to protect its own bond market, sovereign-debt stress is being managed with liquidity - bullish hard assets, bearish fiat.
insights.quote: Long view, US props up the yen to support treasuries.

insights.claim: Visser argues it will be very hard for Kevin Warsh to raise rates while the Fed is being drawn into helping Japan, since defending the yen requires interest-rate differentials, and says he is shocked the market still prices a 45% chance of a September Fed hike and 63% for the BOJ after the payroll number - which is precisely why he likes the debasement trades.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A direct fade of embedded hike odds; the repricing lower is the fuel for gold, silver, platinum and Bitcoin.
insights.quote: we still have a 45% chance of a rate hike in September, which is why I like all the debasement trades, as I talked about a few weeks ago, thinking that people were getting way too over their skis on rate hikes

insights.claim: Visser's 'nothing stops this train' framework holds that governments cannot let long yields run because falling equity values cut corporate tax receipts while deficits run 5-6%, so 30-year yield spikes across the US, UK and JGBs reliably precede official intervention and S&P rallies - July was the biggest 30-year yield rise in a month during Trump's tenure and stocks rallied anyway.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fading the 'bond yields will crash stocks' trade has been persistently profitable because the policy reaction function caps yields and supports equities.
insights.quote: So, the S&P has rallied when rates go higher because everyone starts getting bearish on it and the Fed or the Treasury needs to step in. Nothing stops this train.

themes.theme: Debasement Trades: Gold, Silver, Platinum, Bitcoin

insights.claim: Gold rose 7.2% for the week - the third biggest week in 16 years - and broke back above its 50-day moving average after the third-longest stretch below it, having last been above it in March, a bull-market consolidation-and-breakout pattern Visser says can run hard now that the market is repricing Warsh as less bad for gold.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A defined technical trigger to re-enter gold after months of chop, tied to a specific macro catalyst.
insights.quote: This is a big week in gold, up 7.2%.

insights.claim: Visser sees an absolute reason to own gold, silver, platinum and Bitcoin together assuming the Fed does not hike, with platinum breaking above its 50-day on a rounding chart and silver finally closing above its 50-day, and notes speculative dollar positioning is at its highest long level even though the dollar has already broken down - fuel for the fire for all four.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A basket expression of the debasement view with 50-day entries per metal, plus crowded dollar longs as the forced-unwind accelerant.

insights.claim: Bitcoin remains technically in a bear market until it clears Visser's resistance level, with anything below that a trade rather than an investment, but he expects the level to hold and break out - noting Bitcoin was okay this week despite the Clarity Act's odds of being signed into law this year collapsing from near 50% to 17%, Michael Saylor's Strategy selling more, and a Coldcard cold-storage exploit.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin absorbing three simultaneous negative catalysts without breaking is a resilience tell, and the breakout level defines the risk on the long.
insights.quote: Bitcoin is still in a bear market until we get above there.

themes.theme: Hidden Labor Weakness and Broken Inflation Data

insights.claim: Visser argues economists are missing labor-market weakness because low jobless claims are an artifact of a shrinking labor force - participation has fallen sharply this year - yet wages are not rising: the quits rate and Atlanta Fed median wage growth are back at 2019 levels and average hourly earnings are down to 3.2%, also a pre-2020 level.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Decelerating wages alongside shrinking labor supply hollows out the hawkish case and supports fading September hike odds.
insights.quote: So, the supply of labor is going down because the labor force participation rate is coming down sharply, has come down sharply this year. Well, if there's less labor supply, shouldn't that mean wages are going higher?

insights.claim: Aggregate weekly payrolls - combining weekly hours, average hourly earnings and job creation - just posted their weakest six-month rate of change going back to 2012 excluding COVID, and the only jobs created over the last 18 months have been in healthcare.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The hardest data point behind the dovish rates call and a monthly metric to track for the Fed-repricing trade.
insights.quote: When you strip out healthcare, there is no job creation. That is not a good jobs market.

insights.claim: Visser says AI is already suppressing hiring but has not yet hit firing, and expects no large job-loss event because demographics and voluntary retirements absorb it - instead one-employee million-dollar AI-native companies gradually replace firms with 50 to 100 employees, keeping the labor market structurally weak, with weakness eventually surfacing in either inflation or the AI-driven job market in a way that surprises people.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies a slow-bleed labor market that caps rates - he flags the 10-year's 20-month moving average at 4.29 as the reference line - without a recession-style earnings collapse.
insights.quote: AI agents are have or AI is having an impact on hiring. It's not yet had an impact on firing

insights.claim: Truflation's core measure has made a violent move lower over the last four weeks and keeps falling year-over-year even as core CPI ticks up, leading Visser to call the inflation data a disaster and urge Warsh to weigh Truflation and trimmed mean over a methodology calculated the way it was 50 years ago.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If real-time inflation is collapsing while official CPI lags, the hawkish repricing is a fade and both duration and hard assets win.
insights.quote: This is a violent move lower over the course of the last 4 weeks. So, the year-over-year Truflation number just continues to fall.
